Johannes Piscator
yo-HAHN-es pis-KAH-tor
proper noun (figure)
Latin Johannes — “John,” from Hebrew Yochanan (“the LORD is gracious”). Piscator is the Latin for “fisherman,” a scholarly Latinizing of the German surname Fischer.

Biblical Definition

Johannes Piscator (1546–1625 AD) was a German Reformed theologian and biblical commentator, long the leading light of the Reformed academy at Herborn in Nassau. A prodigious labourer in the Scriptures, he produced commentaries upon the whole Bible and a fresh German translation, and his exegetical works were widely read and esteemed among the Reformed. In much he was sound and useful, a diligent expositor who served the churches by his patient labour in the text. Yet on one weighty head of doctrine Piscator fell into a real and serious error, which must be named plainly: he denied the imputation of Christ’s active obedience to the believer. Where the Reformed churches confess that Christ, as our Surety, both bore the penalty of the law in His sufferings and death (His passive obedience) and also fulfilled the whole righteous demand of the law in His holy life (His active obedience), and that both together are imputed to us for our justification, Piscator taught that only Christ’s passive obedience — His death and satisfaction — is imputed, while His active obedience was owed on His own account and is not reckoned to us. This is no small matter, for it touches the very ground of the believer’s standing before God; and the Reformed churches, at the Synod of Dort and elsewhere, rightly maintained against him the full and complete imputation of the whole obedience of Christ, active and passive alike, as the sole righteousness in which the sinner is accepted. We honor Piscator’s labour in the Scriptures while marking his error where he erred.

Webster 1828 Definition

German Reformed theologian of Herborn (1546–1625 AD); a diligent commentator who denied the imputation of Christ’s active obedience — a real error.

JOHANNES PISCATOR, proper noun. Latin Johannes (“John”) + Piscator (“fisherman,” for German Fischer).

German Reformed theologian and biblical commentator (1546–1625 AD); professor at Herborn in Nassau.

A prodigious expositor of the whole Bible; produced commentaries and a fresh German translation.

Denied the imputation of Christ’s active obedience — holding only His passive obedience is reckoned to us.

Answered by the Reformed churches, who maintain the full imputation of Christ’s whole obedience.

Key Scripture

Rom 5:19 — "For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous."

2Co 5:21 — "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him."

Mat 5:17 — "Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil."

Php 3:9 — "And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith:"

Modern Corruption

A diligent Reformed commentator marred by a real error: his denial of the imputation of Christ’s active obedience.

expand to see more

Piscator’s error must be named, not softened. He held that Christ’s active obedience — His perfect keeping of the law throughout His holy life — was something owed for Himself as a man under the law, and therefore not imputed to believers; only His passive obedience, His suffering and death, he said, is reckoned to us for justification. This cuts at the root of the gospel comfort, for if only the penalty were paid and not the positive righteousness supplied, the sinner would be left merely acquitted of guilt but not clothed in that perfect righteousness which the law requires for life. The Reformed churches rightly answered that Christ, as the second Adam and our federal Head, was not born under obligation to the law for Himself, but voluntarily placed Himself under it for us, and that His whole obedience, active and passive, is one seamless righteousness imputed to all who believe.

This is a genuine doctrinal corruption within the Reformed household, not a matter of tender confessional difference, and it is answered not by appeal to the spirit of the age but by the plain teaching of Scripture: “by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous.” The obedience of Christ that justifies is not truncated but entire. We may honor Piscator’s learning and use his commentaries with profit, even as we reject this his error and hold fast, with the Reformed confessions, to the full and glorious imputation of the whole obedience of our Surety — that the believer is found in Him, not having his own righteousness, but the righteousness which is of God by faith.
